This practice should be adopted for every build, not just the "machine health" builds. Upon completion of the build, the components should be heat-treated to relieve residual stresses, machined off the build plate, and subjected to a comprehensive analysis. This includes density measurements and metallography to determine if full density and complete fusion were achieved. Part-to-part variations in density or microstructure within the build may indicate improper airflow, which can push debris over other parts instead of into the filter system. Mechanical testing should be performed to ensure that the mechanical behavior of the parts falls within the acceptable range for additive manufacturing. Finally, surface roughness measurements should be conducted to assess the consistency and sufficiency of airflow along the entire build platform. Based on the analysis results, any necessary machine adjustments should be made to ensure optimal performance. If required, additional "machine health" builds can be performed to fine- tune the machine's settings until fabrication is consistently repeatable over a series of builds. Only then can the machine be deemed fully qualified. Moreover, regular health monitoring is crucial to maintain optimal performance, particularly in the event of an anomaly, such as an irregularity in the build, machine component replacement, or facility disruption like a power outage. By adopting a proactive approach to machine maintenance and monitoring, manufacturers can ensure that their additive manufacturing machines continue to produce high- quality parts with precision and reliability. UNCLASSIFIED AMMT – 316H SS Los Alamos National Laboratory Page 1-9 1.3 Machine Health Monitoring & Archiving The state of the machine is essential in additive manufacturing, as it directly impacts the quality and reliability of the fabricated parts. To operate at optimal capability, the machine must be in good health, which is influenced by various factors, including regular maintenance between builds, biyearly or yearly preventive maintenance performed by qualified personnel, machine cleanliness, facility conditions, and operator proficiency. Designating machines for specific materials can minimize the risk of cross-contamination, but it's important to regularly inspect and maintain moving components, such as leveling platform gears, recoating arms, and powder dosing dispensers, to ensure they are functioning correctly and in a clean state. These components, comprising gears, motors, and precision motion parts, can wear over time, leading to setup and operational difficulties. While it may not be feasible to visually inspect these components, their proper functioning can be verified by leveling the build platform, moving platforms freely, removing obstructing powder, and cleaning or replacing felt seals.
